Whether imaging detectors flying at heights sufficient to reduce dose rates could out-performlower-flyinghigh-ratedetectorsisanotherquestionthatshouldgovernhardwaredesign selection. 4.4 Nuclear Safeguards The application of SDF toward Nuclear Safeguards would foremost see its use in the quantitative tracking of nuclear material through every step of the fuel cycle in a given facility, but other uses of SDF that support safeguards exist as well. This is predominantly a mission performed by the IAEA, although the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and NNSA nuclear material handling laboratories, plants and sites have safeguards use cases as well. Quantitative safeguards processes can be very challenging for new reactor designs such as pebble-bed and small modular reactors. One specific use of SDF would be to both identify locations of hold-up and to measure the spatial distribution and quantity of nuclear material held up in ducts and process pipes. Hold- up identification using SDF technology has already been demonstrated [8], but higher TRL advancement would be beneficial. Quantification and characterization of hold-up require one to measure dimensions, estimate (or use prior or/and complimentary knowledge) attenuation from the ducts/pipes, and convert measurements into source-strength determinations with associated uncertainty estimates. Mobile SDF platforms can make 3D measurements so dimensions can be measured. Further, due to its ability to move and image from different directions, self-shielding LBNL Report #2001653 issues can be assessed and potentially corrected algorithmically. Such an application would require SDF’s estimation software capabilities to be enhanced with source-estimation capabilities with uncertainty quantification, as well as model-selection, since one may have to impute the type and geometry of the source. The ability to perform the estimation withmultimodaldatae.g.,full-spectralgammaandneutronmeasurements(tocircumventshielding effects), neutron multiplicity effects and gamma/neutron ratios would also be necessary. Since facilities are complex and cluttered environments, being able to incorporate imaging techniques and prior information e.g., in terms of duct/pipe materials and thicknesses will be beneficial in the reconstruction technique. A second specific use of SDF would be in facility design verification. Facilities are required to submit their designs for verification purposes; verification consists of ensuring that the dimensions have been correctly reported. A mobile SDF platform, with lidar and GPS, could be used to measure facility dimensions, and cross-correlate them with the reported one. Such work is the subject of an NA-22 Objective L project [69].
